Use dietary supplements wisely

Which supplements are truly beneficial – and which are not.

Vitamins, minerals, omega-3 – the supplement market is booming. But do you really need all these pills? This guide shows you when dietary supplements make sense, how to recognize quality, and which mistakes to avoid.

Check nutrient status

In short, explained

  • Principle: Test first, then supplement – ​​not the other way around
  • Useful in cases of: Proven deficiency, increased need, restricted diet
  • Common deficiencies: Vitamin D, B12, iron, magnesium, omega-3
  • Pay attention to quality: bioavailability, dosage, reputable manufacturers
  • Caution regarding: overdose, interactions, miracle promises
  • Follow-up: Check blood values ​​again after 3-6 months

Check nutrient status

What are dietary supplements?

A stroll through the drugstore or a glance at an online shop reveals a seemingly endless selection: vitamin D for the darker months, magnesium for cramps, omega-3 for the heart, zinc for the immune system, collagen for the skin – the list of available dietary supplements appears inexhaustible. The market is booming like never before, and Germans now spend over two billion euros annually on these products. But before you plunge into the jungle of supplements, it's worth gaining a basic understanding of what dietary supplements actually are, what they can do – and, above all, what they can't do.

Dietary supplements, or NEM for short, are by definition products intended to provide nutrients in concentrated form. They come as tablets, capsules, powders, drops, or effervescent tablets and contain vitamins, minerals, amino acids, fatty acids, fiber, or so-called phytochemicals. The crucial point is already in the name: they are meant to supplement , not replace, a normal diet. This distinction may sound trivial, but it is misunderstood or ignored by many people. A supplement is not a substitute for a balanced diet, just as a bandage cannot heal a broken leg.

The gray area between food and medicine

Legally, dietary supplements exist in an interesting gray area. They are not classified as medicines, but as food – with all the consequences that entails. Unlike medicines, there is no mandatory approval before sale, no standardized efficacy testing, and significantly less stringent controls. The responsibility for safety and the accuracy of the information largely lies with the manufacturer. This doesn't mean that all dietary supplements are unsafe or ineffective – but it does mean that you, as a consumer, must take more responsibility and cannot blindly trust that a product will deliver on its promises.

This legal classification also has implications for advertising. Dietary supplements are not allowed to make any health claims. Statements like "cures diabetes" or "prevents cancer" are prohibited. Instead, so-called health claims are used, meaning permitted health-related statements such as "contributes to the normal function of the immune system." These claims are strictly regulated and must be scientifically substantiated—but they say nothing about whether you personally would benefit from the product. A nutrient can only contribute to normal function if you didn't have enough of it beforehand.

The central question is: Do I even need this?

This brings us to the heart of the problem with modern supplement culture. Advertising suggests that practically everyone could benefit from supplements – more energy, better sleep, brighter skin, a stronger immune system. The reality is different: Supplements can correct an existing deficiency, but they cannot improve an excess. If your vitamin D levels are already optimal, additional vitamin D will not make you healthier. If you get enough magnesium from your diet, magnesium tablets will not prevent cramps you wouldn't have anyway.

This doesn't mean that dietary supplements are generally useless. It means that their usefulness depends on your individual situation. A vegan who doesn't supplement with vitamin B12 is highly likely to develop a deficiency because B12 is practically non-existent in plant-based foods. A woman with heavy menstrual bleeding might benefit from iron supplementation because she loses more than she can absorb through her diet. An office worker who sees little daylight in winter could develop a vitamin D deficiency. But the average person who eats a reasonably balanced diet and has no particular risk factors probably needs fewer supplements than advertising would have them believe.

Why this guide is important

In the following sections, you'll learn when dietary supplements can actually make a difference and when they're a waste of money. You'll find out which nutrients are frequently deficient in Germany and for whom supplementation is worthwhile. You'll learn to recognize quality and not be blinded by marketing. And above all, you'll learn the only truly reliable approach: test first, then act strategically, then monitor. Because at the end of the day, it's not about swallowing as many pills as possible, but about giving your body what it actually needs – nothing more and nothing less.

When supplements are useful

The question of whether you need dietary supplements can't be answered with a simple yes or no. It depends on your individual situation – your diet, lifestyle, stage of life, genetic predisposition, and any existing medical conditions. Nevertheless, there are clear situations where supplementation actually makes a difference, and others where it's, at best, a waste of money. Understanding this distinction is key to using dietary supplements wisely.

The clearest case: Proven deficiency

The clearest indication for supplementation is a laboratory-confirmed deficiency that cannot be corrected, or not quickly enough, through dietary changes alone. If your blood test shows that your vitamin D level is 10 ng/ml, while the optimal range is 40-60 ng/ml, then it is practically impossible to correct this deficiency in a reasonable timeframe simply through increased sunlight or vitamin D-rich foods. In such cases, supplementation is not optional—it is medically necessary to avoid adverse health consequences.

The situation is similar with iron deficiency, which can manifest itself through symptoms such as fatigue, paleness, and difficulty concentrating. While you can increase your iron intake through iron-rich foods like red meat, legumes, or pumpkin seeds, in cases of severe deficiency with depleted stores (low ferritin), replenishing iron through diet alone would take months—time during which you would continue to suffer from the symptoms. An iron supplement can help much more quickly in such cases, but supplementation should be discussed with a doctor, as iron overdose can be harmful.

Increased need due to special life situations

There are phases of life and circumstances that increase nutritional needs so significantly that meeting them through a normal diet becomes difficult or even impossible. Pregnancy is the classic example: The need for folic acid rises dramatically in the first few weeks – even before many women know they are pregnant. Since a folic acid deficiency during this critical phase increases the risk of neural tube defects in the unborn child, doctors recommend that women planning a pregnancy begin folic acid supplementation before conception. Waiting until a deficiency is measurable would be negligent.

Even intense exercise can increase nutritional needs to an extent that is difficult to meet through diet alone. Endurance athletes lose significant amounts of electrolytes such as sodium, magnesium, and potassium through sweat. During long training sessions or competitions, especially in hot weather, replenishment through food and water alone may not be sufficient to compensate for these losses. In such situations, electrolyte supplements are not a marketing ploy, but a sensible tool for maintaining performance and promoting health.

People who, due to their work or lifestyle, see little daylight—shift workers, office employees who commute to and from work in the dark during winter—have a significantly increased risk of vitamin D deficiency. In Germany, the sun's intensity from approximately October to March is insufficient to enable any significant vitamin D production in the skin. For these groups, winter vitamin D supplementation is advisable as a preventative measure, without having to wait for a deficiency to develop.

Limited intake or restrictive diet

Certain diets make it virtually impossible to obtain sufficient amounts of individual nutrients. Veganism is the most prominent example: Vitamin B12 is found in relevant quantities exclusively in animal products. There is no discussion, no alternative, no exception – anyone following a vegan diet must supplement B12. Anything else will sooner or later lead to a deficiency with potentially serious neurological consequences, some of which are irreversible. This is not a weakness of veganism; it is simply a fact that must be accepted and acted upon accordingly.

Even with a vegetarian diet, the intake of certain nutrients such as iron, zinc, and omega-3 fatty acids can be borderline, depending on how carefully the diet is planned. General supplementation is not always necessary, but regular blood tests are recommended to detect potential deficiencies early.

Gastrointestinal disorders can significantly impair nutrient absorption. People with celiac disease absorb fewer nutrients through their damaged small intestine. Patients with Crohn's disease or those who have undergone stomach surgery experience similar problems. Certain medications can also affect absorption: proton pump inhibitors, prescribed for heartburn, reduce the absorption of vitamin B12 and magnesium. In all these cases, targeted supplementation is often part of medical care.

When supplements are not useful

The most common mistake when it comes to supplementation is believing that a handful of pills can compensate for a poor diet. 'I eat a lot of fast food, but I take a multivitamin' – this way of thinking fundamentally misses the point of a healthy diet. Supplements can never replace the complex matrix of nutrients, fiber, phytochemicals, and not-yet-fully-understood synergies that real food provides. An apple is more than the sum of its vitamins, and no capsule in the world can replace a meal made from fresh ingredients.

The most important nutrients at a glance

Not all nutrients are equally relevant when it comes to supplementation. Some are sufficiently obtained through diet by the majority of the population, while deficiencies in others are so widespread that targeted supplementation is indeed beneficial for many people. In this section, you'll learn which nutrients are worth a closer look and what you should know about each one.

Vitamin D – The perennial favorite among supplements

Vitamin D occupies a special position among dietary supplements because it differs fundamentally from other vitamins. Strictly speaking, it is not a vitamin in the classical sense, but a precursor to a hormone that the body can produce itself in the skin when exposed to sufficient sunlight. The problem is that in Germany and other countries north of the 42nd parallel, the intensity of sunlight from about October to March is insufficient to produce significant amounts. Even in summer, most people spend too much time indoors, use sunscreen, or cover their skin, so the body's own production often remains inadequate.

The consequence: According to estimates, around 60 percent of the German population has suboptimal vitamin D levels, although the definition of 'optimal' is certainly open to debate. The Robert Koch Institute assumes that approximately 30 percent of adults have an actual deficiency. The effects are manifold: Vitamin D plays a central role in bone health, the immune system, muscle function, and possibly also mood. A severe deficiency can lead to fatigue, muscle weakness, and, in the long term, to osteoporosis.

The recommendation for most people is to supplement in winter, typically with 1000 to 2000 IU per day, which corresponds to the amount that would be produced with moderate sun exposure. In summer, if you spend enough time outdoors, you may be able to forgo supplementation. If you are unsure or belong to a risk group—dark skin pigmentation, being overweight, older age, little time spent outdoors—a blood test is advisable to determine your actual status.

Vitamin B12 – essential for a vegan diet, important for many others

Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin that plays an essential role in cell division, blood formation, and the function of the nervous system. What makes it particularly important from a supplementation perspective is that it is found in significant quantities almost exclusively in animal products. Meat, fish, eggs, and dairy products are the relevant sources; plant-based foods contain at best trace amounts or inactive analogues that the body cannot utilize.

For vegans, there's no question: B12 supplementation is mandatory, not optional. Anyone who follows a vegan diet and doesn't supplement with B12 will very likely develop a deficiency within a few years. This can initially manifest in nonspecific symptoms – fatigue, difficulty concentrating, paleness – and, if left untreated, can lead to neurological damage, some of which is irreversible. This isn't scaremongering, but a medical reality that every vegan should know and take seriously.

But other groups are also at risk: vegetarians who consume few eggs and dairy products; older people, whose absorption of B12 from food decreases due to reduced stomach acid production; people with gastrointestinal diseases; and those who regularly take proton pump inhibitors or metformin. For these groups, at least regular monitoring of B12 status is recommended, ideally using the marker holotranscobalamin, which is more sensitive than simple serum B12.

Iron – Common deficiency, but cautious supplementation is advised.

Iron deficiency is the most common nutrient deficiency worldwide and in Germany particularly affects women of childbearing age, pregnant women, and people who follow a vegetarian or vegan diet. The body needs iron for oxygen transport in the blood, energy production, and numerous enzymatic processes. A deficiency manifests itself through chronic fatigue, difficulty concentrating, paleness, hair loss, and increased susceptibility to infections – symptoms that, however, can also have many other causes.

Unlike vitamin D, caution is advised with iron: the body has no effective way of getting rid of excess iron. Too much iron can accumulate in organs and cause damage. People with the genetic disorder hemochromatosis are particularly at risk, but unnecessary or excessive iron supplementation can also be problematic for others. Therefore, a strict rule applies: iron should only be supplemented if a deficiency has been proven, not "on suspicion" or "just to be safe." A blood test that measures ferritin and transferrin saturation will provide information about your iron status.

Magnesium – The anti-stress mineral

Magnesium is involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions in the body and plays a role in muscle and nerve function, energy production, blood sugar regulation, and bone health. A deficiency often manifests as muscle cramps, sleep problems, restlessness, and headaches—although, again, these symptoms can have many causes. Studies indicate that a significant portion of the population does not meet the recommended magnesium intake, particularly during periods of stress, high alcohol consumption, and intense exercise, all of which increase magnesium requirements.

Magnesium supplementation is relatively safe, as excess magnesium is excreted via the kidneys. However, high doses can cause diarrhea, which some consider a natural 'stop mechanism'. When supplementing with magnesium, pay attention to the form: magnesium citrate and magnesium glycinate are absorbed significantly better than the cheaper magnesium oxide.

Omega-3 fatty acids – for heart and brain

The long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA are important for heart health, brain function, and the regulation of inflammatory processes in the body. They are found in significant amounts primarily in fatty fish – salmon, mackerel, herring, and sardines. While the body can theoretically convert the plant-based omega-3 fatty acid ALA from flaxseed oil or walnuts into EPA and DHA, this conversion rate is very low, making it a poor source.

Those who eat fewer than two portions of fatty fish per week – and this applies to the majority of the German population – may benefit from omega-3 supplementation. For vegans and vegetarians, there are algae oil supplements that provide EPA and DHA directly, without the intermediate step of obtaining them from fish. The overall data on the health benefits is positive, even though individual studies show mixed results.

Recognizing quality – what to look for?

The dietary supplement market is enormous, and the quality differences between products are significant. While some supplements are formulated to a high standard and deliver on their promises, others contain underdosed or poorly absorbed ingredients, questionable additives, or don't even match the information on the label. As a consumer, you're in a difficult position: without access to a laboratory, you can't verify a product's quality yourself. That's why it's so important to know the markers that indicate quality—and the warning signs that should raise suspicion.

The problem with regulation

To understand why quality differences can be so significant, one must understand the legal classification of food supplements. In the European Union, they are considered food, not medicine. This has far-reaching consequences: unlike medicines, there is no mandatory approval process before they can be placed on the market. Manufacturers only need to register their product with the Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, but are not required to submit proof of efficacy or comprehensive safety studies. The authorities conduct random checks, but systematic testing does not take place.

This regulatory gap doesn't mean all dietary supplements are unsafe – in fact, the vast majority aren't. But it does mean that quality depends heavily on the individual manufacturer, and that as a buyer, you can't blindly trust that a product contains what it claims to, in the stated quantity, and in a form your body can actually absorb. That's why it's worth taking a closer look.

Bioavailability – Not every form is equally good

A nutrient isn't simply a nutrient. The same substance can exist in different chemical forms that vary considerably in their bioavailability – that is, how well the body can absorb and utilize it. Inexpensive products often use the cheapest forms, which may technically contain the nutrient, but are poorly absorbed by the body.

Let's take magnesium as an example: Magnesium oxide is the cheapest form and has a high elemental content, but only about 4 percent is absorbed by the intestines – the rest ends up unused in the stool. Magnesium citrate, on the other hand, is absorbed much better, as is magnesium glycinate, which is also particularly well-tolerated and, when taken in the evening, can even improve sleep quality. The price difference is real, but so is the difference in actual nutrient absorption.

Similar differences exist for many other nutrients. For vitamin B12, methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin are the active forms that the body can use directly, while cyanocobalamin must first be converted. With zinc, zinc picolinate and zinc citrate have better bioavailability than zinc oxide. For iron, iron bisglycinate is significantly gentler on the stomach than classic ferrous sulfate. When buying a supplement, it's worth paying attention to the form used – not just the quantity.

Dosage – The art of the right measure

Another quality indicator is dosage. Some products are chronically underdosed: they contain so little of the advertised nutrient that any effect is unlikely. This is particularly common with combination products and proprietary blends, where expensive ingredients are added in microdoses simply to be listed on the label. Other products are overdosed and exceed the recommended upper limits, which can be especially problematic with fat-soluble vitamins and some minerals.

The recommendations of the German Nutrition Society (DGE) serve as a guideline, representing the lower limit for what is considered beneficial, while the Upper Intake Level (UL) of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) represents the upper limit for what is still considered safe. A good supplement falls within this range, although the optimal dose depends on your individual circumstances – which is why a blood test before supplementation is so valuable.

Additives – Less is often more

A glance at the ingredient list reveals a lot about a manufacturer's philosophy. Some products contain a long list of additives in addition to the actual active ingredient: fillers, flow agents, coating agents, colorings, sweeteners, and flavorings. Not all of these additives are problematic—some are technically necessary for tablet production—but many are. Titanium dioxide, for example, long used as a whitening agent, is now banned in food but can still be found in some supplements. Artificial colors and flavorings are unnecessary and problematic for some people.

High-quality products are characterized by short, easy-to-understand ingredient lists. They avoid unnecessary additives and, where technically possible, use plant-based or natural excipients. If you don't understand a product's ingredient list or if it's longer than the actual active ingredient content, that's a sign to look elsewhere.

Characteristics of reputable providers

Since you, as a consumer, cannot personally verify the quality of a product in a laboratory, you are dependent on the trustworthiness of the supplier. Reputable manufacturers are characterized by transparency: They provide precise dosages, name the chemical forms used, list all ingredients, and do not make exaggerated advertising claims. Many have their products tested by independent laboratories and make the certificates of analysis available upon request or directly on their website.

Be wary of products with "secret formulas" or "proprietary blends" where the exact quantities aren't specified. Unrealistic advertising claims—"Boost your immune system by 500%," "guaranteed weight loss," "anti-aging miracle"—are also red flags. And while a very low price might indicate inferior ingredients, a high price is no guarantee of quality—sometimes you're just paying for the marketing.

Common mistakes in supplementation

Even with the best intentions, many people make mistakes when taking dietary supplements that undermine their effectiveness, waste money, or, in the worst case, harm their health. Most of these mistakes have a common denominator: they stem from ignorance, belief in marketing promises, or the understandable but misguided desire to "play it safe." Below, you'll learn about the most common pitfalls and how to avoid them.

Flying blind: Supplementing without diagnostics

By far the most common and consequential mistake is taking dietary supplements without first having your nutritional status determined through a blood test. This mistake has several dimensions: First, without a test, you don't know if you even have a deficiency that needs addressing. Symptoms like fatigue, difficulty concentrating, or hair loss can indicate a nutrient deficiency—but also dozens of other causes, from thyroid problems and sleep deprivation to psychological stress. If you take iron tablets because you feel tired, but your ferritin level is normal, you haven't solved the problem and may have created a new one.

Secondly, without a baseline level, you don't know what dose is appropriate. A mild vitamin D deficiency requires different supplementation than a severe one. Thirdly, without follow-up tests, you can't assess whether the supplementation is working or whether you need to adjust the dose. And fourthly—especially important with nutrients like iron, which can be harmful in overdose—you might be supplementing something you don't need and that could be detrimental to your health.

The solution is simple and makes everything easier in the long run: Have the relevant values ​​checked before starting any supplementation. Supplement specifically with what's missing, in a dose that matches the degree of deficiency. And check after a few months whether the strategy is working.

The 'more is more' paradox

A common misconception is: if 1000 IU of vitamin D is good, then 10,000 IU is better. If 200 mg of magnesium helps, then 800 mg will help even more. This way of thinking stems from the understandable desire to get the maximum benefit from supplementation, but it ignores a fundamental principle of nutritional physiology: for most nutrients, there is an optimal range, and more than optimal is not better—it is potentially harmful or at least useless.

With water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C and the B vitamins, the body excretes what it doesn't need through urine. Mega-doses of these vitamins, therefore, produce, at best, expensive urine. However, with fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K, as well as minerals like iron, zinc, and selenium, the body cannot simply get rid of excess amounts. They accumulate and can become toxic. Vitamin A overdose can cause liver damage and is harmful to the fetus during pregnancy. Too much iron increases the risk of oxidative stress and is life-threatening for people with a genetic iron storage disease. Too much selenium leads to selenosis with hair loss and neurological symptoms.

The rule is: Supplement to correct a deficiency or meet an increased need – not to reach theoretical maximum levels. The dose should be based on your individual condition, not on marketing claims or the desire for 'optimization'.

Ignore interactions

Dietary supplements are often perceived as harmless because they are not prescription drugs. This perception is dangerously wrong. Supplements contain biologically active substances that can interact with other supplements and medications—sometimes with serious consequences.

Some practical examples: Vitamin K affects blood clotting and can counteract the effects of blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin), increasing the risk of thrombosis and stroke. St. John's wort, a popular herbal remedy for low mood, accelerates the breakdown of numerous medications in the liver, including birth control pills, immunosuppressants, and HIV medications—with potentially dramatic consequences. Calcium can hinder the absorption of certain antibiotics and thyroid medications. Iron and zinc compete for absorption in the intestines and should not be taken at the same time.

The consequence: Inform your doctor about all dietary supplements you take – not just prescription medications. If you regularly take medication, research possible interactions or consult a pharmacist before adding a new supplement.

The supplement-as-an-excuse trap

A psychologically interesting but health-related mistake is using supplements as an excuse for an otherwise unhealthy lifestyle. 'I eat a lot of fast food, but I take my multivitamin.' 'I don't get to exercise, but I take my omega-3 capsules for my heart.' These rationalizations feel plausible, but are fundamentally wrong.

Dietary supplements cannot compensate for a poor diet. Nor can they counteract lack of exercise, sleep deprivation, or chronic stress. The health benefits of real foods—vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts—extend far beyond their isolated nutrients. The complex matrix of fiber, phytochemicals, enzymes, and not-yet-fully-understood synergies cannot be contained in a capsule. A head of broccoli is more than the sum of its vitamins.

Supplements should be exactly what their name suggests: additions to an already solid foundation. If the foundation is shaky, the problem lies with the foundation itself – not the missing supplement.

Falling for marketing

The dietary supplement industry is a marketing industry. Behind terms like 'detox', 'boost', 'anti-aging', 'superfood', or 'clinically tested', there's often more advertising than science. Influencers who enthusiastically rave about a product usually do so for payment. Testimonials and before-and-after pictures prove nothing. And the fact that a product is 'natural' says nothing about its effectiveness or safety.

Stay critical. Ask yourself about every supplement: Does it have a scientifically plausible mechanism of action? Are there high-quality studies on humans (not just cell cultures or animal experiments)? Do I actually need this nutrient? And: Who benefits if I buy this product? When in doubt, your money is better invested in high-quality food, exercise, and good sleep than in the latest miracle supplement.

Supplements for specific target groups

While the principles of smart supplementation apply to everyone, certain population groups have specific or increased nutritional needs that warrant special attention. These groups either have an increased risk of deficiencies, a physiologically heightened requirement, or limitations that make it difficult to obtain sufficient nutrients through a normal diet. If you belong to one of these groups, you should be aware of the following recommendations—and ideally, verify them with regular blood tests.

Vegans and Vegetarians – The Classics

People who abstain from animal products face specific challenges regarding nutrient intake. By far the most significant of these concerns vitamin B12: Anyone who follows a vegan diet and does not supplement with B12 will develop a deficiency – not possibly, not perhaps, but almost certainly. B12 is found in relevant quantities exclusively in animal products, and the widespread claims about plant-based B12 sources such as algae or fermented products are, unfortunately, largely myths. The B12 analogs contained in these products cannot be utilized by the human body, or only insufficiently.

For vegans, B12 supplementation is therefore not a recommendation, but a necessity. A daily dose of 250-500 µg or a higher weekly dose are common strategies. Since vitamin B12 is water-soluble and the body can only absorb limited amounts at one time, regular smaller doses are more effective than infrequent mega-doses.

Besides vitamin B12, there are other nutrients that can be critical in a plant-based diet: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) are not found in plant-based foods; their conversion from the plant precursor ALA is inefficient. Algae oil supplements are the vegan solution here. Iron and zinc from plant sources are absorbed less efficiently than those from animal sources, which can be partially compensated for by clever combinations (e.g., vitamin C with iron-rich meals), but makes regular monitoring of levels advisable. Iodine can become deficient if dairy products and fish are omitted and non-iodized salt is used.

For vegetarians who still consume eggs and dairy products, the situation is less critical. With sufficient consumption of these products, vitamin B12 requirements are usually met, and other critical nutrients are also easier to obtain. Nevertheless, an annual blood test is recommended to identify individual deficiencies.

Pregnant and breastfeeding women – providing for two

Pregnancy is the phase of life with the highest nutritional needs. The growing fetus and the preparation of the mother's body for childbirth and breastfeeding increase the need for virtually all micronutrients – sometimes so drastically that meeting these needs through normal diet alone becomes difficult.

Folic acid is paramount: it is essential for cell division and the development of the neural tube, from which the brain and spinal cord develop. A deficiency in the first weeks of pregnancy—often before the woman even knows she is pregnant—significantly increases the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Therefore, it is recommended to begin folic acid supplementation as soon as a woman is planning a pregnancy, typically with 400–800 µg daily.

Iron is needed in increased amounts during pregnancy for the formation of the fetal blood volume and the placenta. Many women who previously had borderline iron stores develop a pronounced deficiency during pregnancy. However, supplementation is only advisable in cases of proven or impending deficiency – prophylactic iron supplementation can lead to constipation and other side effects.

Iodine is important for the thyroid function of both mother and child, and therefore for the fetus's cognitive development. DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid, supports brain development. Vitamin D remains important, as it is in the general population. Most gynecologists recommend special pregnancy supplements containing these nutrients in a balanced combination – however, they emphasize that high doses of vitamin A during pregnancy can be harmful to the fetus and should therefore not be consumed in excess.

People over 60 – Changed rules of the game

With increasing age, the rules governing nutrient supply change in several ways. The intestinal capacity for absorption decreases, particularly for vitamin B12: The production of stomach acid and intrinsic factor, which are necessary for B12 absorption, declines with age, so that even with sufficient dietary intake, a functional deficiency can occur. Regular B12 monitoring and, if necessary, supplementation are therefore recommended for older people – at higher doses than for younger people, since absorption is less efficient.

The skin's ability to produce vitamin D under the influence of sunlight also decreases. At the same time, older people often spend less time outdoors. This combination results in a significantly increased risk of vitamin D deficiency, which is particularly problematic in old age as it exacerbates the already increasing risk of osteoporosis and falls. Supplementation during the winter months is advisable for most people over 60, and year-round if sun exposure is limited.

Calcium and vitamin D together are important for bone health – a topic that becomes particularly relevant for women after menopause, when the protective effect of estrogen on bones diminishes. Finally, protein intake becomes more important with age: the body utilizes protein less efficiently, so a higher intake is needed to maintain muscle mass. While this isn't a typical supplement topic, it's part of the overall picture of nutritional needs in old age.

Athletes – Increased throughput

Regular, intensive training increases nutritional needs on several levels. The higher energy expenditure also means a greater need for micronutrients involved in energy metabolism. Sweat loss leads to electrolyte losses, particularly sodium, but also magnesium and potassium. And certain sports—especially endurance sports—are associated with specific nutrient losses, such as the so-called 'runner's iron deficiency' caused by microscopic blood loss in the gastrointestinal tract and the mechanical destruction of red blood cells.

Regular iron monitoring is advisable for endurance athletes, especially for female athletes who experience additional losses due to menstruation. Electrolyte supplements are more than just marketing during long training sessions in the heat – they can maintain performance and prevent cramps. Creatine is one of the most thoroughly researched supplements and has been proven to improve performance in strength training and high-intensity exercise. And while protein supplements aren't essential – most athletes can meet their protein needs through their diet – they offer convenience when a protein-rich meal isn't readily available.

What you should avoid

In an industry driven by marketing and less strictly regulated than the pharmaceutical market, there are products that are useful at best, useless, and at worst, dangerous. Some dietary supplements are aggressively advertised even though their effectiveness is unproven or the risks outweigh the potential benefits. This section will tell you which product categories and ingredients warrant particular caution—not to alarm you, but to help you invest your money and your health more wisely.

Overdosed individual nutrients without medical indication

A supplement claiming to contain '1000% of the daily requirement' of a vitamin sounds like a particularly good product at first glance. In reality, it's often the opposite: a product that is ineffective at best and harmful at worst. With water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C or the B vitamins, the body simply excretes what it doesn't need through urine – you're producing expensive urine. The situation is more serious with fat-soluble vitamins and minerals.

High doses of vitamin A are hepatotoxic and can cause birth defects in pregnant women. Therefore, vitamin A is one of the vitamins for which overdosing is explicitly discouraged, especially during pregnancy. Vitamin E was long considered harmless until large-scale studies showed that high doses increase the risk of bleeding and may even increase overall mortality. Selenium has a very narrow range between optimal and toxic levels – supplementation without prior assessment is risky. And iron, as already mentioned, does more harm than good in people who are not deficient.

The rule of thumb is: Mega-doses of individual nutrients belong in the hands of doctors who are treating a specific deficiency, not in the everyday lives of people who simply want to 'do something good for themselves'.

Proprietary blends and 'secret formulas'

If a product label states "Proprietary Blend"—a proprietary mixture where the ingredients are listed but not their quantities—this is a clear warning sign. This practice allows manufacturers to add expensive active ingredients in tiny, ineffective amounts just to list them on the label, while the majority of the mixture consists of cheap fillers.

You might end up paying for a 'brain booster supplement' that advertises ginkgo, bacopa, and phosphatidylserine on the label, without knowing whether the amounts it contains even come close to the dosages that have shown effects in studies. Reputable manufacturers have no secrets from their customers – they provide precise amounts because they have nothing to hide.

'Detox' products and liver cleanses

The detox market is a multi-billion dollar business built on a fundamental misunderstanding: the idea that 'toxins' accumulate in the body and must be eliminated through special products, juices, or cleanses. Scientific reality is different: your body has highly efficient detoxification organs in the form of your liver and kidneys, which work around the clock – without needing the support of expensive powders or questionable cleanses.

Most detox products are harmless and ineffective: They contain fiber, herbal extracts, or vitamins that, at best, serve as expensive placebos. Some, however, are more problematic: They contain hidden laxatives or diuretics that produce short-term weight loss through water and stool loss, but do not actually detoxify the body and can be harmful with regular use. Your money is much better invested in a balanced diet that doesn't burden your liver.

Fat burners and appetite suppressants

The hope of losing weight effortlessly with a pill is understandable – and is ruthlessly exploited by the supplement industry. 'Fat burners' are products that supposedly boost metabolism and increase fat burning. In practice, most of these products contain caffeine in varying amounts, sometimes combined with other stimulants such as synephrine or herbal extracts with questionable effects.

The problem: The effect on actual calorie expenditure is minimal – we're talking about perhaps 50-100 calories per day, if that. That's equivalent to half an apple. The side effects, however, can be significant: rapid heartbeat, high blood pressure, sleep disturbances, and anxiety. There have been documented cases of cardiac arrhythmias and even deaths associated with high-dose fat burners. The only sustainable way to lose weight is through a moderate calorie deficit and exercise – no shortcut in the world can change that.

Testosterone booster and muscle-building miracle

For men who desire more muscle, more energy, or an improved libido, 'natural testosterone boosters' hold a tempting promise. The reality is sobering: the vast majority of over-the-counter products in this category have no demonstrable effect on testosterone levels. Ingredients such as Tribulus terrestris, D-aspartic acid, or ashwagandha have been studied, and the results are mixed at best, often negative.

If your testosterone is truly low, that's a medical issue requiring a doctor's evaluation and, if necessary, prescribed therapy – not supplements from the internet. And if your testosterone is normal, no supplement will increase it.

Anti-aging miracle cure

NMN, NAD+ precursor, resveratrol, spermidine – the anti-aging supplement scene is full of promising-sounding substances. Indeed, there is interesting basic research on some of these substances, often with impressive results in cell cultures or animal models. The problem: Translating these findings to humans is uncertain, long-term data is lacking, and the optimal dosages are unclear. What works in a mouse doesn't necessarily work in a human, who also has a completely different metabolic profile.

This doesn't mean these substances are ineffective – only that the evidence for their use in humans is not yet sufficient. If you want to invest money in longevity, you're on the safer and probably more effective side with the tried-and-tested basics – regular exercise, a balanced diet, sufficient sleep, and stress management.

The right approach: Test, supplement, control

After everything you've learned so far about dietary supplements—when they make sense, which nutrients might be relevant, and which mistakes to avoid—the question remains: How do you put it all into practice? The answer lies in a systematic, data-driven approach that replaces guesswork with knowledge and allows you to continuously optimize your supplementation. This approach can be broken down into four steps: determining your baseline, interpreting the results, supplementing strategically, and monitoring your progress.

Step 1: Determine your starting point

The first and most important step is determining your current nutrient status through a blood test. Without this baseline, you're essentially flying blind – you won't know if a deficiency exists at all, how severe it is, or which nutrients are actually affected. A good basic check should include the nutrients that are commonly deficient in the German population and can be influenced by supplementation.

Vitamin D, measured as 25-hydroxyvitamin D, is the most important parameter – deficiency is epidemic in our latitudes. Vitamin B12 should ideally be measured as active B12 or holotranscobalamin, as these markers indicate a deficiency earlier and more reliably than simple B12 in serum. If iron deficiency is suspected or if the individual belongs to a risk group, ferritin is the most informative value – it shows the level of iron stores, not just the iron currently circulating in the blood. Folic acid is particularly relevant for women trying to conceive, and thyroid levels can help rule out symptoms that may resemble nutrient deficiencies but have a different cause.

Depending on the individual situation, other parameters may be useful: the Omega-3 Index if there is interest in Omega-3 intake, magnesium in whole blood if corresponding symptoms are present, zinc or selenium if specific risk factors are present. Not everything needs to be measured for everyone – but what is measured should be selected with a specific goal in mind.

Step 2: Interpreting the results correctly

Having a lab result is the first step; understanding it correctly is the second. Many people – and even some doctors – make the mistake of considering any value that is 'within the normal range' as optimal. This interpretation is too simplistic. Normal values ​​are determined statistically: they show where 95 percent of the population falls, not where you function best. A value can be normal and still be suboptimal.

Let's take vitamin D as an example: Many laboratories define the normal range as starting at 20 ng/ml because below this threshold, bone damage is a risk. However, this doesn't mean that 20 ng/ml is optimal – many experts consider the target range to be closer to 40-60 ng/ml. The situation is similar with ferritin: A value of 15 µg/l is still considered normal, but for someone experiencing symptoms of fatigue, it might be too low to feel truly well.

Ideally, you should discuss your results with a doctor or nutritionist who is knowledgeable in this area and doesn't just read the reference values, but puts them into the context of your symptoms and lifestyle. If you can't or don't want to do that, at least familiarize yourself with current scientific discussions on optimal ranges – they often differ from the reference values ​​on the lab report.

Step 3: Targeted supplementation

Based on your test results, you can now decide what to do. In the case of a true deficiency, the solution is clear: you supplement the missing nutrient in a dose that corresponds to the severity of the deficiency. A severe vitamin D deficiency initially requires higher doses than a mild one; borderline ferritin needs a different strategy than a pronounced iron deficiency.

For values ​​that are within the normal range but not optimal, you have more leeway. Here you should consider: Do I have symptoms that could explain this suboptimal value? Do I belong to a risk group for this nutrient? Can I improve the value through dietary changes, or is supplementation the more practical approach? A slightly low omega-3 index in someone who already wanted to eat more fish might not require supplementation – but it would for a vegan.

If a value is good – really good, not just normal – then you don't need a supplement for that nutrient. Even though it's tempting to play it safe, further increasing an optimal value through supplementation offers no benefit and, in the case of some nutrients, carries risks.

Step 4: Monitor and adjust success

Supplementation isn't a one-time thing, but an iterative process. After you start supplementing, you should retest after a few months – typically three to six. This check serves several purposes: It shows you whether the supplementation is having the desired effect. It helps you adjust the dose – you might need more, you might need less. And it prevents you from slipping into the overdose range.

Depending on the result, you adjust your strategy. Has the deficiency been corrected and the level is now optimal? Then you can potentially switch to a lower maintenance dose. Has the level barely increased? Then the dose may be too low, the bioavailability of the product poor, or there may be an absorption problem that should be investigated. Has the level exceeded the target? Then reduce the dose or take a break.

This feedback loop – test, supplement, monitor, adjust – is the core of smart supplementation. It distinguishes conscious action from guesswork and ensures that you actually benefit from your supplements.

Check your status

After everything you've learned about supplements, one question naturally arises: How do you find out where you personally stand? The answer is less complicated than you might think. A blood test can provide clarity within a few days about which nutrients you have in sufficient quantities, which are borderline, and which should actually be supplemented. This knowledge is the foundation for any sensible supplementation decision – without it, you're operating in the dark.

Why a test makes the difference

Symptoms like fatigue, difficulty concentrating, hair loss, or frequent infections can indicate a nutrient deficiency—but they can also have a hundred other causes. Fatigue can stem from iron deficiency, but also from thyroid problems, sleep apnea, depression, or simply chronic sleep deprivation. Without testing, any supplementation remains a guess, a shot in the dark. You could spend money on supplements you don't need while the actual deficiency goes undetected.

A blood test takes the guesswork out of the equation. It shows you not only whether a deficiency exists, but also which nutrient is affected and how severe the deficiency is. This information is crucial for the correct dosage: A severe vitamin D deficiency requires a different strategy than a mild one. And it protects you from unnecessary supplementation of nutrients you already have adequate levels of.

Which values ​​should be tested?

A sensible basic check of your nutrient supply includes parameters that are frequently deficient in Germany and can be influenced by supplementation. First and foremost is vitamin D – by far the most common nutrient deficiency in our latitudes, especially during the winter months. Vitamin B12 is important for everyone who eats few or no animal products, as well as for older people and those taking certain medications. The iron level, measured as ferritin, indicates the state of your iron stores and is particularly relevant for women of childbearing age. Folic acid is essential for women trying to conceive, but is also a useful indicator for others.

Additionally, it can be helpful to have your thyroid levels checked. Thyroid dysfunction can cause symptoms that are easily mistaken for nutritional deficiencies – fatigue in hypothyroidism, weight changes, mood swings. Ruling out the thyroid before experimenting with supplements can save you a lot of trouble.

One-time test or regular testing?

An initial test gives you a baseline—a starting point from which to work. This first test is the most important because it shows you where you stand before you change anything. If you begin supplementing based on the results, you should retest after three to six months to see if the strategy is working and if adjustments are needed.

If values ​​remain stable and lifestyle is unchanged, an annual check is usually sufficient. Exceptions include situations involving significant changes: a change in diet, a new life phase such as pregnancy, the start of intensive exercise, illness, or new symptoms. In these cases, an additional test may be useful to determine whether the changed circumstances have also affected nutritional status.

Conclusion – Supplementing Smartly

This guide concludes with a simple yet crucial insight: dietary supplements are neither superfluous nor indispensable – their usefulness depends entirely on your individual circumstances. In a world where marketing tries to convince us that we all need a dozen different pills to be healthy, this nuanced perspective is more important than ever. The truth, as is so often the case, lies somewhere in between: some people benefit significantly from targeted supplementation, while others simply waste their money.

Key findings at a glance

The guiding principle throughout this guide is: test first, then supplement. Without a blood test that reveals your actual nutrient status, any supplementation is a shot in the dark. You don't know if you have a deficiency, you don't know which nutrient is affected, and you don't know what the appropriate dose would be. A test costs a fraction of what you could spend on unnecessary supplements over the course of a year – and gives you the peace of mind that you're doing the right thing.

Quality matters more than quantity. A high-quality product with good bioavailability and transparent labeling is preferable to any cheap product, even if it costs more. What good is inexpensive magnesium oxide that your body barely absorbs, when the more expensive magnesium citrate actually provides what you need? Look for bioavailable forms, reputable manufacturers, and realistic dosages – and don't be fooled by marketing promises.

More isn't always better. For almost all nutrients, there's an optimal range, and exceeding this range offers no benefit and can even be harmful. This is especially true for fat-soluble vitamins and minerals like iron and selenium, which can accumulate in the body. The dosage should be based on your individual needs, not on the desire to "play it safe" or "do something good."

Supplements complement, they don't replace. No pill in the world can replace a balanced diet of fresh, unprocessed foods. The complex matrix of nutrients, fiber, phytochemicals, and not yet fully understood synergies that real food offers cannot be packed into a capsule. Those who lay their foundation with good nutrition need fewer supplements—and the few they do need are more effective.

Your practical timetable

If you're unsure how to proceed after reading this guide, here's a simple roadmap: Start with a blood test that covers the most important parameters – vitamin D, B12, ferritin, folic acid, and, if necessary, thyroid levels. Review the results, not only in relation to the reference values ​​but also in the context of your symptoms and lifestyle. Supplement specifically where a deficiency or borderline level exists, using high-quality products in appropriate dosages. And check after three to six months whether the strategy is working.

This cycle – test, supplement, monitor, adjust – is the core of smart supplementation. It distinguishes informed action from guesswork, prevents both under- and over-supplementation, and ensures that every euro you spend on supplements actually delivers a benefit. In an industry that is often more marketing than science, this evidence-based approach is your best protection against making the wrong choices.

Dietary supplements can be a valuable part of your health strategy – if you use them correctly. With the knowledge from this guide, you're now able to make informed choices instead of blindly following the next trend. Use this knowledge, and your body will thank you.
